section.title: Misery, Then Hope
section.sectionRationale: The book ends where honesty must begin: in the wreckage of a society where no one upright is left and even the family turns on itself. Yet from that darkness rises one of the great confessions of faith, but as for me, I will look to the LORD. The chapter climbs to a soaring finish, who is a God like You, who pardons iniquity and casts our sins into the depths of the sea, keeping the covenant sworn to Abraham. The prophet's own name, which means who is like the LORD, becomes the last note of the book.
section.thesis: When society and even the household have collapsed, the believer's hope is not in people but in the God of salvation who hears; and the God who is beyond compare pardons iniquity, tramples it underfoot, and casts every sin into the sea, keeping the covenant love He swore to Abraham, fulfilled in Christ.
section.frameNote: Three movements: Israel's great misery, where the godly have vanished and a person's enemies are his own household (1-6); the confession and comfort of the one who waits for the God of salvation in the dark (7-13); and the closing prayer and doxology, who is a God like You who pardons iniquity and casts our sins into the sea, keeping faith to Abraham (14-20).

verses.text: Woe is me! For I am like one gathering summer fruit at the gleaning of the vineyard; there is no cluster to eat, no early fig that I crave.
The godly man has perished from the earth; there is no one upright among men. They all lie in wait for blood; they hunt one another with a net.
Both hands are skilled at evil; the prince and the judge demand a bribe. When the powerful utters his evil desire, they all conspire together.
The best of them is like a brier; the most upright is sharper than a hedge of thorns. The day for your watchmen has come, the day of your visitation. Now is the time of their confusion.
Do not rely on a friend; do not trust in a companion. Seal the doors of your mouth from her who lies in your arms.
For a son dishonors his father, a daughter rises against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law. A man’s enemies are the members of his own household.

units.label: I will wait for the God of my salvation
units.note: though I fall, I will rise

verses.text: But as for me, I will look to the LORD; I will wait for the God of my salvation. My God will hear me.
Do not gloat over me, my enemy! Though I have fallen, I will arise; though I sit in darkness, the LORD will be my light.
Because I have sinned against Him, I must endure the rage of the LORD, until He argues my case and executes justice for me. He will bring me into the light; I will see His righteousness.
Then my enemy will see and will be covered with shame, she who said to me, “Where is the LORD your God?” My eyes will see her; at that time she will be trampled like mud in the streets.
The day for rebuilding your walls will come, the day for extending your boundary.
On that day they will come to you from Assyria and the cities of Egypt, even from Egypt to the Euphrates, from sea to sea and mountain to mountain.
Then the earth will become desolate because of its inhabitants, as the fruit of their deeds.

units.label: Who is a God like You
units.note: He casts our sins into the sea

verses.text: Shepherd with Your staff Your people, the flock of Your inheritance. They live alone in a woodland, surrounded by pastures. Let them graze in Bashan and Gilead, as in the days of old.
As in the days when you came out of Egypt, I will show My wonders.
Nations will see and be ashamed, deprived of all their might. They will put their hands over their mouths, and their ears will become deaf.
They will lick the dust like a snake, like reptiles slithering on the ground. They will come trembling from their strongholds in the presence of the LORD our God; they will tremble in fear of You.

{{mikamokha|Who is a God like You}}, who {{nasa|pardons iniquity}} and passes over the transgression of the remnant of His inheritance, who does not retain His anger forever, because He delights in {{chesed|loving devotion}}?
He will again have compassion on us; He will vanquish our iniquities. You will cast out all our sins into the depths of the sea.
You will show {{emet|faithfulness}} to Jacob and loving devotion to Abraham, as You swore to our fathers from the days of old.

mikamokha.gloss: Who is like You? The book closes with a question that is really the highest praise. The prophet's own name, Micah, is a shortened form of Mikayahu, meaning who is like the LORD; so the whole book ends by sounding out his name in worship. The same cry rang at the Red Sea, who is like You among the gods, and here it marvels not at God's power but at His matchless mercy in pardoning sin.

nasa.gloss: To lift, carry, bear away. To pardon iniquity is literally to lift it off and carry it away, the same picture as bearing a burden or removing guilt. It is the language of the scapegoat carrying sin into the wilderness and points forward to the One who bears away the sin of the world, taking our guilt upon Himself and carrying it off for good.

chesed.gloss: Steadfast love, covenant loyalty, loving devotion. Rendered here loving devotion, it names the loyal, merciful love that keeps covenant. God does not retain anger forever because He delights in chesed; His mercy is not reluctant but joyful. This is the same chesed His people were told to love in 6:8, now revealed as the very thing God most delights to show.

emet.gloss: Faithfulness, truth, reliability. God will show faithfulness to Jacob and loving devotion to Abraham, keeping the very oath He swore to the patriarchs centuries before. The final ground of hope is not the people's goodness but God's unbreakable covenant truth, His faithfulness to His own promise, which reaches its yes in Christ.

basic.context: Micah looks around and grieves: it is as though the harvest is over and there is not one good grape or fig left. The godly have vanished, leaders take bribes, and you cannot even trust your closest friend or family; a person's enemies are those in his own house. Yet in that darkness the prophet plants his feet: but as for me, I will look to the LORD, I will wait for the God of my salvation. He owns his sin, trusts God to plead his case, and then the book rises to a breathtaking finish: who is a God like You, who pardons sin and casts it into the depths of the sea, keeping the promise He made to Abraham long ago.
basic.hermeneutics: The chapter moves in three steps: honest lament over a corrupt society, a confession of faith in the dark, and a closing hymn of praise to the pardoning God. Verse 6 is quoted by Jesus about the division the gospel brings. The great ending, verses 18 to 20, is not wishful thinking but rests on God's sworn covenant with Abraham, which the New Testament says is kept in Christ. The name Micah itself, who is like the LORD, becomes the last word of praise.
basic.originalLanguages: The climax turns on the prophet's own name. Mi kamokha, who is like You, echoes his name Micah, who is like the LORD. God pardons iniquity, the verb nasa, to lift and carry sin away. He delights in chesed, loyal covenant love, the same word from 6:8. And He shows emet, faithfulness, to Jacob and Abraham, keeping His sworn word.
basic.typology: The God who lifts and carries away sin foreshadows the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world. Casting sin into the depths of the sea points to the total, irreversible forgiveness secured at the cross. And the covenant sworn to Abraham is fulfilled in Christ, the seed of Abraham in whom all nations are blessed.
basic.christ: Micah 7:18-20 is the gospel in seed form. God pardons iniquity by lifting it off and carrying it away, and He does this finally in Jesus, who bears our sin in His body on the tree. Our sins are cast into the sea, never to be dredged up, and the promise to Abraham finds its yes in Christ, the offspring in whom the nations are blessed.
basic.god: God is shown as utterly beyond compare, not chiefly in raw power but in mercy: He pardons, passes over transgression, does not keep His anger forever, and delights, actually delights, in showing loyal love. He is faithful to promises made centuries earlier to Abraham. He is a Shepherd who tends His flock, and a Redeemer whose forgiveness is as deep and final as the sea.
basic.crossReferences: Jesus quotes Micah 7:6 in Matthew 10:35-36 about the division He brings. Exodus 15:11 asks who is like You among the gods, the same cry of wonder. Psalm 103:12 pictures sins removed as far as east from west, and Isaiah 53 shows the Servant bearing away our iniquity, fulfilled in Christ, the seed of Abraham of Galatians 3.
basic.oneStory: The book ends by facing the worst, a world without one upright person, and then lifting its eyes to the only hope: the incomparable God who pardons sin, tramples it down, and buries it in the sea. This is the God who keeps faith with Abraham, and the whole promise runs forward to Christ, in whom sin is carried away and every nation is blessed.

context.literary:
Micah 7 is one panel of a three-fold cycle that organises the whole book. Chapters 1 to 3 pronounce judgment, chapters 4 and 5 turn to restoration, and the cycle begins again at 6:1 with judgment that runs through 7:6 before the final hope of 7:7 to 20. The last chapter therefore plays the book's pattern in miniature, and it ends on the hopeful side of the pattern, not the dark side.

The voice keeps changing, and that is the key to reading it. Verses 1 to 6 are the prophet's own lament, introduced by 'Woe is me!' Verses 7 to 10 are a personal confession of faith, but the enemy who taunts in verse 10 is a woman, 'she who said to me,' so the speaker sounds like the daughter of Zion speaking for the whole faithful remnant, not only for one man. Verses 11 to 13 turn and address the city with a promise. Verses 14 to 17 begin as a prayer to the Shepherd, and in verses 15 to 17 God Himself answers in the first person, 'I will show My wonders.' Verses 18 to 20 then turn to praise, and the pronouns widen to 'us' and 'our fathers.' The chapter reads like a service in which the people, the prophet and God take turns.

The courtroom frame matters as well. In 6:1 and 6:2 the LORD brought a case against His people. In 7:9 the people say they will bear His anger 'until He argues my case,' and the same legal picture is now turned toward their defence. The Judge who prosecuted in chapter 6 is the advocate who pleads in chapter 7. The chapter also opens with an image of a field picked clean after harvest and closes with sins drowned in the sea, so it moves from scarcity to a mercy that has no bottom.
context.historical:
Micah came from Moresheth, a town in the lowland of Judah near the Philistine frontier, 1:1 and 1:14. He prophesied under Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah, so his hearers watched Assyria swallow the north. Samaria fell in 722 BC, and in Hezekiah's fourteenth year Sennacherib took the fortified towns of Judah, 2 Kings 18:13. The Assyrian envoy standing outside Jerusalem boasted that he had come up against the city under the LORD's own word, 2 Kings 18:25. That is the world behind the taunt of verse 10, 'Where is the LORD your God?'

Verses 2 to 6 sketch a society in which every restraint has failed. Justice is for sale, 'the prince and the judge demand a bribe,' verse 3, and the village, the one place a person could count on loyalty, has become a place of surveillance. In an honour and shame culture built on clan and household, to be told that a man's enemies are in his own house was to be told the ground itself had given way.

The promise of verses 11 and 12 has two horizons. Walls would be rebuilt, which presumes they will first fall, and Micah elsewhere says the people will go to Babylon and be redeemed there, 4:10. Jeremiah's elders remembered that Micah had said Zion would be plowed like a field and that Hezekiah's repentance had turned the disaster aside, Jeremiah 26:18 and 19. People coming 'from Assyria and the cities of Egypt' names the two great powers of Micah's day as the ends of the exile, and Isaiah 11:16 uses the same road from Assyria. Bashan and Gilead, verse 14, were the pastures east of the Jordan that Israel took under Moses, Numbers 21:33 to 35, and that Tiglath-pileser stripped away, 2 Kings 15:29. The prayer asks for the lost land back.
context.canonical:
Jesus takes up Micah 7:6 in Matthew 10:35 and 36 and again in Luke 12:51 to 53. He does not say that dividing households is His aim. He says it is what His coming will bring out, in a world where allegiance to Him costs people their closest ties, and He lets the prophet's description of a collapsing society stand as a description of discipleship under pressure. In Luke 19:44 He weeps that Jerusalem 'did not recognize the time of your visitation,' using the word that sits in Micah 7:4, the day of visitation that the watchmen should have seen coming.

The taunt 'Where is the LORD your God?' is a stock mockery of the faithful, found in Psalm 42:3, Psalm 79:10 and Joel 2:17. The warning 'Do not gloat' has its counterpart in Obadiah 12 and Proverbs 24:17 and 18. The Shepherd prayer of verse 14 grows into Ezekiel 34:23, the one shepherd David, and then into John 10:11 and Hebrews 13:20, where Jesus is the good and the great Shepherd. The nations licking the dust like a snake in verse 17 recalls the serpent's sentence in Genesis 3:14, and Paul's promise that God will 'crush Satan under your feet,' Romans 16:20.

The closing hymn is stitched from Exodus 34:6 and 7, the same confession that Joel 2:13, Jonah 4:2 and the very next book, Nahum 1:3, each take up in their own way. The oath 'to our fathers' in verse 20 comes back in the song of Zechariah, who says God has remembered His holy covenant, 'the oath He swore to our father Abraham,' Luke 1:72 and 73. Paul says Christ confirmed the promises made to the patriarchs so that the Gentiles might glorify God for His mercy, Romans 15:8 and 9, and the second half of that sentence is Micah's own horizon of verse 12, nations streaming in.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Micah is writing to people who may be tempted to conclude one of two things: that the situation is so bad that God must have left, or that the situation is so bad that nothing can be done and faith should go quiet. The chapter refuses both. It tells the truth about corruption in chapters 1 to 6 without softening it, and then models what a believer does while the corruption is still in place. He does not retreat into cynicism, he does not pretend the leaders are better than they are, and he does not deny his own share in the guilt. He says 'I have sinned' and then 'I will wait.'

The prophet also wants his hearers to see that waiting is not passive. The false watchmen of verse 4 had looked for a different kind of day, and the day of visitation caught them unprepared. The prophet's own posture in verse 7 is the true watcher's, eyes toward the LORD. He expects the ending to be a vindication that comes from God and not from the exiled people's own strength, and he gives the community words to pray in the meantime: shepherd us, show us wonders as in the days of Egypt, and remember Abraham.

The closing hymn is meant to end the book on wonder. Micah has indicted, threatened and promised for seven chapters, and the last word is a question no one can answer except by pointing at God. The hearer is meant to leave not with a theory of forgiveness but with a person to praise.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Much of this chapter is description in the first person, and it should be read as a prayer to join and not as a rulebook to apply. The statement that you should not trust a friend or a companion in verse 5 describes the temper of a society where trust has failed. It does not tell believers to treat their spouse as a suspect, and it is not a general principle of how to live in a family. The advice to seal the doors of the mouth is bitter irony about how far things had gone.

The lament, by contrast, is a pattern to imitate. Verses 7 to 9 show how to hold sorrow and confidence together: wait on the LORD, accept the discipline as just, expect Him to plead your case, and refuse to gloat when your enemy falls. The statement that the enemy will be trampled, verse 10, is a promise about God's justice and not a licence for retaliation, which is why the same speaker begins by saying 'Do not gloat over me.'

The forgiveness hymn is both a proclamation about God and an invitation. It tells us what God is like, and it also sets the terms on which God can be approached: not on merit, but because He delights in loving devotion. Readers today are not asked to reproduce the exile, but to pray the way Micah prays, and to trust the same character.

debates.question: Is the great forgiveness of 7:18-20 grounded in Israel's repentance or in God's own character and covenant?

views.label: Grounded in God's character and sworn covenant
views.case: The text roots pardon in who God is, He delights in chesed, and in the oath sworn to Abraham and Jacob from the days of old, not in the people's worthiness, which the chapter has just shown to be bankrupt. The hymn gives no condition at all. It lists what God does, in the future tense, as a settled intention.

views.label: Repentance is the necessary channel
views.case: The confession of verse 9, 'Because I have sinned against Him,' shows that pardon is received by those who own their guilt and wait on God, so repentance is the appointed way mercy is embraced. Other prophets set forgiveness beside return, as in Isaiah 55:7.

debates.bearing: Scripture holds both: forgiveness flows from God's free, covenant-keeping character and is received by those who, like the prophet, confess their sin and look to the God of their salvation, a mercy secured once for all in Christ.

debates.question: Who is speaking in verses 7 to 10?

views.label: The prophet himself
views.case: The first person singular runs unbroken from verse 1, 'Woe is me,' through verse 7, 'But as for me.' Micah has already spoken of himself in this way in 3:8, and the line 'Do not gloat over me, my enemy' fits a man who shares the fate of his people.

views.label: Zion or the faithful remnant, personified
views.case: The enemy in verse 10 is feminine, 'she who said to me,' and the speaker 'sits in darkness' and has 'fallen,' language that fits a city or nation in exile more than one man. The woman Zion was already addressed in 4:10 as one who would go to Babylon and be redeemed there. On this reading the prophet gives voice to the whole community.

views.label: Both at once
views.case: Prophets regularly speak as representatives. Micah can be the lone believer and the mouthpiece of the remnant in the same breath, so that his confession becomes the one every exiled believer is invited to make.

debates.bearing: The reading barely changes the sense, but it changes who is invited in. If the speaker is Zion, then the confession of sin and the vow to wait are the community's own words, and every later believer who prays them joins that choir.

debates.question: What does verse 11 promise?

views.label: Rebuilt walls and a wider border
views.case: The BSB reads 'the day for rebuilding your walls will come, the day for extending your boundary.' The following verse supports this, since people stream to the city from every direction, which suggests growth and ingathering.

views.label: A decree reaching far away
views.case: The Hebrew word for boundary can also mean a decree, and some take the line to say that on that day a decree, God's edict of restoration, will go far out. The idea is still restoration, but its focus is God's word and not territory.

debates.bearing: Both readings point to the same event, God rebuilding what judgment destroyed. The difference is whether the picture is spatial or declarative, and neither alters the hope.

study.originalLanguages:
The chapter has a vocabulary of waiting that deserves slow reading. In verse 4 the 'watchmen' and in verse 7 the prophet's resolve to 'look' to the LORD come from the same Hebrew root, the verb to keep watch. The watchmen of Israel, the prophets and leaders who should have been scanning the horizon, watched only for their own profit, and the day of their 'visitation' came, from the root paqad, to attend to or to call to account. The one true watcher is the man who says 'I will look to the LORD.' Habakkuk 2:1 uses the same verb for a prophet standing on the ramparts to see what God will say. Verse 7 adds that he will 'wait,' and that verb, which has a sense of hoping with expectation, is the one in Lamentations 3:24, 'therefore I will hope in Him.'

The 'God of my salvation' in verse 7 contains the root yasha, to deliver. It is the root behind the names Joshua and Jesus, and it means rescue from a tight place, which is why Matthew 1:21 can explain the name with 'He will save His people from their sins.' Micah's hope is already shaped like the name that would one day be given.

Verse 2 says people 'hunt one another with a net,' and the word for net, cherem, is spelled exactly like the word for an offering devoted to destruction. A dangerous word of hunting ends up describing a society that devotes its own to ruin. The 'godly man' who has perished is the chasid, from the root of chesed, the loyal, covenant-keeping person. In verse 2 the chasid is gone, and in verse 18 the chesed of God is what remains. When the human supply of loyalty runs out, God's does not.

The court language of verse 9 uses the root rib, to plead a lawsuit, the same word God used in 6:2 when He had a case against His people. In the same verse the 'righteousness' the speaker will see is tsedaqah, here God's saving rightness, His putting things right for those who wait.

The three words for sin in verses 18 and 19, iniquity, transgression and sin, are the same triad in Exodus 34:7, where God is 'forgiving iniquity, transgression, and sin.' The Hebrew verb for 'pardons,' nasa, means to lift up and carry, and it is the verb used of the goat that bears the people's iniquities away on the Day of Atonement, Leviticus 16:22. The verb 'passes over' is the same used in Proverbs 19:11, where it is a person's glory to overlook an offence.

The verb translated 'vanquish' in verse 19 is kavash, to subdue, the word used when humanity is told to 'subdue' the earth in Genesis 1:28. Sin is treated as a conquered thing, trodden down. The compassion God shows is rachamim, which comes from the word for the womb, the tenderness of a mother for her child. The sea into which sins are cast calls up the Red Sea, where Pharaoh's army 'sank there like a stone,' Exodus 15:5. Sins receive the treatment of Egypt's pursuing army.

Finally, verse 20 gives 'faithfulness' to Jacob and 'loving devotion' to Abraham, reversing the order of what each man was known for. Jacob, the schemer, receives emet, truth or reliability, and Abraham, the one called by grace, receives chesed. God is dependable toward the unreliable heir and loving toward the one who started it.

typology.type: The goat that carries iniquity away, Micah 7:18
typology.fulfillment: The verb for 'pardons' in verse 18 is the verb used when the scapegoat bears Israel's iniquities into the wilderness, Leviticus 16:22. The prophet's picture of God lifting sin and carrying it off is therefore built from the vocabulary of the sacrificial system. In Christ the correspondence deepens: the Lamb of God 'takes away the sin of the world,' John 1:29, and He 'bore our sins in His body on the tree,' 1 Peter 2:24. Isaiah 53:6 says the LORD laid on the Servant the iniquity of us all. The type falls short because the goat was a symbol and the sin returned each year, while Christ carries it once and forever.

typology.type: Sins hurled into the depths, like Pharaoh's army, Micah 7:19
typology.fulfillment: Exodus 15:4 and 5 sings of Pharaoh's chariots cast into the sea, where 'the depths have covered them,' and Nehemiah 9:11 says God hurled the pursuers 'into the depths like a stone.' Micah applies that exodus image to guilt: God deals with sin as He dealt with the army that was about to destroy His people. In Christ the sea becomes baptism, in which believers are buried with Him and raised, Romans 6:4, and Colossians 2:13 and 14 says the debt against us was cancelled and 'nailed to the cross.' The picture is limited because the Egyptians' bodies washed up, Exodus 14:30, while Micah's sins are gone from sight.

typology.type: The Shepherd of verse 14 and the days of Egypt
typology.fulfillment: The people pray that God would shepherd them with His staff in Bashan and Gilead 'as in the days of old,' and God promises wonders 'as in the days when you came out of Egypt,' verse 15. The exodus becomes the pattern for a future rescue. Jesus claims the title: 'I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down His life for the sheep,' John 10:11, and Hebrews 13:20 says God brought back from the dead 'that great Shepherd of the sheep' through the blood of the eternal covenant. The new exodus is not from Egypt or Babylon but from sin and death, Luke 9:31. The type falls short because Israel's pastures were a strip of land; Christ's flock comes from every nation.

People come to the restored city from Assyria and Egypt, the very powers that had crushed Israel. Micah 4:1 to 4 had already pictured the peoples streaming to the mountain of the LORD. That ingathering is met in the church, when Gentiles are brought near, Ephesians 2:17, and Paul says Christ became a servant to confirm the promises to the patriarchs so that the Gentiles might glorify God for His mercy, Romans 15:8 and 9. The type is incomplete: the nations come to a city in Micah, but in the New Testament they come to a person, and in Revelation 21 to a city whose temple is the Lamb.

study.christ:
Micah 7 leads to Christ most directly through the figure of the one who waits and is vindicated. The speaker sits in darkness, endures anger that he is willing to call just, and declares that the LORD 'will be my light.' The book that began with Samaria's ruin does not end with a human champion but with the God of his salvation. The Gospel of John makes the light claim in the first person, 'I am the light of the world,' John 8:12, and the New Testament presents Jesus as the one in whom the darkness of verse 8 gives way to the light of verse 9.

The chapter also prepares the idea that God Himself will be the advocate for the guilty. In verse 9 the people expect to endure the LORD's anger because they have sinned, 'until He argues my case.' The Judge who brought the lawsuit in chapter 6 becomes the one who pleads. The New Testament gives the shape of how: Christ is the one who died, was raised, and 'is interceding for us,' Romans 8:34, and God acts 'so as to be just and to justify the one who has faith in Jesus,' Romans 3:26. The lawsuit does not vanish; its verdict falls on the Son. Paul says God made Him who knew no sin 'to be sin on our behalf, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God,' 2 Corinthians 5:21, and that is the 'righteousness' Micah says the waiting people will see.

The closing hymn is gospel in seed form for a particular reason. It says God will 'again have compassion' and 'cast out all our sins,' and it grounds that in an oath, not in a transaction. The oath is the one sworn to Abraham, and Paul says the promise was spoken to Abraham's 'seed,' meaning one, who is Christ, Galatians 3:16, so that those who belong to Him are heirs, Galatians 3:29. Zechariah in Luke 1:72 and 73 explicitly connects the arrival of Jesus with remembering 'the oath He swore to our father Abraham.' The covenant that Micah leans on is kept in the birth Micah himself announced earlier, the ruler from Bethlehem Ephrathah, Micah 5:2.

There is a bearing-away of sin that Micah can say only in future tense. How can a just God pass over transgression and not retain His anger? Micah does not explain, and Romans 3:25 and 26 does: God put forward Christ as the atoning sacrifice so as to be just and the justifier, having passed over sins committed beforehand. Isaiah 53:11 says the righteous Servant 'will justify many, and He will bear their iniquities.' What Micah praises as a character trait is paid for at the cross.

A caution keeps the reading honest. Micah does not name Jesus here, and the details of the sea, the staff and the woodland are not coded predictions. The path from the chapter to Christ runs through the promises it relies on, the shepherd it asks for, and the forgiveness it describes, each of which the New Testament says is fulfilled in Him.
study.god:
The God of Micah 7 is first shown as one who is present when He seems absent. Verses 1 to 6 describe a world in which no one is trustworthy, and the taunt of verse 10 assumes the LORD has gone quiet. The chapter does not answer by arguing that God was there all along. It answers by having the prophet say 'My God will hear me,' verse 7. The doctrine of God here is first of all that He listens, and that waiting on Him is rational because He has already shown what He does.

He is just, and the chapter does not hide this. The prophet accepts 'the rage of the LORD' as the consequence of his own sin, verse 9, and the vision of verse 13 says the earth will become desolate 'as the fruit of their deeds.' Divine anger in Micah is not a mood but a response to actual wrong. Yet the same verse insists that the anger has an end: 'until He argues my case.' His wrath is real and it is limited.

He is the God who acts in history in a way that echoes the exodus. Verse 15 says that He will 'show My wonders' as in the days of Egypt, which tells us the exodus is not a past event only but the template of how God works: He sees His people stuck, and He comes down. He is also sovereign over the nations, who 'will see and be ashamed,' verse 16, so the faith of the remnant is not just that God cares for them but that He is Lord of the powers that oppress them.

The hymn gives the central portrait. He is incomparable, 'Who is a God like You,' and the incomparability is located not in raw power but in the pardon of sin. He does not retain His anger forever, 'because He delights in loving devotion.' The motive is in Himself, not in the sinner. He is also tender, with the compassion of rachamim, and He is faithful, keeping an oath made centuries before the people he is now rescuing were born. The three words for sin and the three verbs of removal, vanquish, cast, forgive, tell us He deals with sin comprehensively.

This chapter holds together truths that are often set against each other. God is angry and God delights in mercy. He disciplines and He pleads the case of the disciplined. He keeps His covenant and He deals with individuals. The way these hold together is the story the rest of the Bible tells, and Micah is content to praise before he can fully explain.

For worship the chapter teaches us to pray honestly and end in wonder. The lament comes first and is not hurried; the faith of verse 7 is stated in the middle of the dark; and the book closes on a question whose only answer is worship. Nothing in the chapter invites us to be impressed with ourselves, and everything invites us to be amazed at Him.

crossReferences.note: The book's earlier courtroom scene, where the LORD brings a case against His people. Chapter 7 returns to the same legal picture in verse 9, when the people say they will bear His anger until He argues their case. The Judge who accused in chapter 6 is the advocate hoped for in chapter 7, which shows how the whole closing section of the book hangs together.

The foundation of the closing hymn. Here God proclaims Himself compassionate, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion, and forgiving iniquity, transgression and sin. Micah 7:18 and 19 reuse the triad of sin words and ask who is like this God. The hymn is Exodus 34 sung by a people who have seen how much they need it.

Pharaoh's chariots and army are cast into the sea, where the depths covered them and they sank like a stone. Micah 7:19 applies that victory to guilt, saying God will cast out all our sins into the depths of the sea. What God did to the force that enslaved Israel He promises to do to the sin that enslaves her.

Jesus quotes Micah 7:6 to explain that following Him will divide households. The prophet's lament about a family turned against itself becomes a picture of the cost of discipleship. Jesus does not celebrate the division but warns His followers it will come, and tells them it is the world's response to Him, not an accident.

A close parallel to the hymn's themes. God is slow to anger and does not always accuse, He has not dealt with us according to our sins, and 'as far as the east is from the west, so far has He removed our transgressions from us.' It describes with a different image the same removal Micah pictures by the sea.

Another prophet who takes the watchman's post. Habakkuk stands on the rampart to see what God will say, using the same verb as Micah's 'I will look to the LORD' in 7:7. The two prophets show the same posture in a time of violence, which is not despair or denial but a watchful, expectant waiting on God.

Faith rising out of the ruins in the same key as Micah 7:7. The writer calls to mind that the LORD's mercies are new every morning, and that it is good to wait quietly for His salvation. Like Micah, Jeremiah's lament moves from loss to hope by fixing on God's loving devotion, not on circumstances.

God speaks of Himself as the one who blots out transgressions 'for My own sake' and remembers sins no more. This is the same motive as Micah's 'because He delights in loving devotion': forgiveness comes from God's own character, not from the sinner's merit, and it is complete.

Zechariah's song reads Jesus' coming as God remembering His holy covenant, the oath He swore to Abraham. The wording picks up Micah 7:20, 'as You swore to our fathers from the days of old.' The Gospel writer presents the promise Micah leaned on as arriving in the child to be born.

Explains how God can pass over sins and still be just. Micah praises the God who 'passes over the transgression of the remnant,' and Paul says that this passing over was held until God put forward Christ as the atoning sacrifice, so that He might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith.

Quoting the new covenant promise of Jeremiah 31:34, Hebrews says God will remember sins and lawless acts no more. Micah's image of sins in the sea and the later promise of no remembrance say the same thing in two registers, and Hebrews says it is fulfilled in the once-for-all offering of Christ.

study.oneStory:
Micah 7 answers a question that every earlier chapter of the Bible's story has been asking: after the fall, after Babel, after Sinai broken at the foot of the mountain, after Samaria, is there anything on the other side of judgment? The garden had ended in exile in Genesis 3, and the Torah had ended with the warning that exile would come, but also with the promise that God would remember. Micah is the point at which the remnant says out loud what that remembering will look like.

The chapter gathers the main threads of the story. The serpent's sentence of dust in Genesis 3:14 comes back when the nations lick the dust in verse 17, so the enemy of the garden is among those humbled. The exodus pattern returns, with wonders for a people held down by a great power. The covenant with Abraham is the stated ground of hope: God swore to the fathers, and the promise is not held up by the failings of the descendants. The Shepherd of Psalm 23 is asked to lead again. The city that had been taken is promised walls.

The chapter also looks ahead. The next voice in the canon of the Twelve is Nahum, who takes the same description of God from Exodus 34 and applies it to Nineveh, the empire that Micah feared. The forgiveness Micah praises is not for Israel alone. People come in from Assyria and Egypt, verse 12, and the nations are ashamed and humbled before the LORD, verses 16 and 17. The book that opened with a warning about Samaria and Jerusalem finishes by looking beyond them, to a worldwide ingathering.

In Jesus the story arrives. The ruler from Bethlehem of 5:2 comes, the shepherd lays down His life, the Servant bears iniquity, and the oath to Abraham is fulfilled in his seed. Sin is dealt with at the cross and not merely overlooked, and the people of every nation are brought in, Galatians 3:29. The church lives between the promise and its fullness. It has the confession of verse 9 and the light of verse 8, but still sees the world of verses 2 to 6.

The new creation is the end of that world. Revelation 21:4 says there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain, and the corrupt cities of verse 3 are replaced by the city where God dwells with people. The last verse of Micah, 'as You swore to our fathers from the days of old,' is answered when the promise is finally seen to have been kept in every detail.

sermon.title: Parenting with Hope in the Worst of Times
sermon.why: Piper preaches Micah 7, moving from the collapse of society and the family in verses 1 to 6 to the steadfast confidence of verse 7, but as for me I will look to the LORD, and on to the God who bears away iniquity and casts our sins into the sea, showing how hope holds even in the darkest times because of God's incomparable, covenant-keeping mercy.

quiz.q: How does Micah describe the society in verses 1 to 6?

options.text: As so corrupt that the godly have vanished and even one's own household cannot be trusted.
options.note: The harvest is empty of good fruit; leaders take bribes and family turns on family.

options.text: As basically healthy with only a few minor problems.
options.note: The picture is total collapse, not minor problems.

options.text: As already destroyed and completely uninhabited.
options.note: People remain, but trust and godliness have collapsed among them.

options.text: As a model community for the nations to imitate.
options.note: It is the opposite: a warning of moral freefall.

quiz.q: What is the turning point in verse 7?

options.text: But as for me, I will look to the LORD and wait for the God of my salvation.
options.note: In the darkness the prophet fixes his hope on God, not on people.

options.text: The prophet decides to trust his friends and family after all.
options.note: He has just said not to trust even them; his hope turns to God alone.

options.text: The enemy finally offers a peace treaty.
options.note: The shift is inward and Godward, not a treaty with enemies.

options.text: The prophet gives up hope entirely.
options.note: This is the opposite of giving up; it is confident waiting on God.

quiz.q: What does it mean that God pardons iniquity in verse 18?

options.text: He lifts our sin off and carries it away, the picture behind the Hebrew verb nasa.
options.note: To pardon is to bear the guilt away, pointing to the Lamb who takes away the world's sin.

options.text: He merely ignores sin as if it did not matter.
options.note: He does not ignore sin; He carries it away, and justice is met in Christ.

options.text: He requires the people to carry their own guilt forever.
options.note: The point is that God Himself lifts and removes the guilt.

options.text: He pardons only those who have never sinned.
options.note: He pardons the guilty remnant, those who have sinned and confess it.

quiz.q: Why is the ending built on the word who is a God like You?

options.text: It sounds out the prophet's own name and marvels at God's matchless mercy in forgiving sin.
options.note: Micah means who is like the LORD; the book ends by turning his name into praise for God's mercy.

options.text: It is a complaint that God is far away and unlike anyone helpful.
options.note: It is wonder and praise, not complaint; God is near and merciful.

options.text: It asks the nations to name their own gods.
options.note: It celebrates the LORD's incomparable mercy, not rival gods.

options.text: It expresses doubt that God can forgive at all.
options.note: It is confident praise that God does pardon and cast sin into the sea.

quiz.q: On what does the final promise of forgiveness ultimately rest?

options.text: On God's own character and the covenant love He swore to Abraham, fulfilled in Christ.
options.note: Hope rests on God's faithfulness to His oath, kept in Christ the seed of Abraham.

options.text: On the people's proven goodness and reliability.
options.note: The chapter has just shown their goodness is bankrupt; hope rests on God.

options.text: On the strength of the rebuilt city walls.
options.note: Rebuilt walls are a sign of restoration, not the ground of forgiveness.

options.text: On the defeat of the surrounding nations by force.
options.note: The ground is God's covenant mercy, not military victory.

questions: Micah grieves that he cannot find one upright person. When the world around you feels morally bankrupt, where are you tempted to put your hope, and how does verse 7 redirect it?
But as for me, I will look to the LORD. What would it look like this week to wait on the God of your salvation instead of on people or circumstances?
The prophet says, though I have fallen, I will arise; though I sit in darkness, the LORD will be my light. Where do you need that confidence right now?
God pardons iniquity by lifting it off and carrying it away, casting our sins into the sea. Do you live as though your sins are truly gone, or do you keep dredging them back up?
God does not merely tolerate mercy, He delights in it. How does knowing that God delights to forgive change the way you come to Him with your sin?

translationNotes.note: A man's enemies are the members of his own household is cited by Jesus in Matthew 10:35-36; see also Luke 12:53, describing the division the gospel can bring within families.

Who is a God like You (mi kamokha) plays on the prophet's own name, Micah, a shortened form of Mikayahu, who is like the LORD. Forms of the Hebrew chesed, rendered loving devotion, range across love, kindness, faithfulness, mercy, and covenant loyalty.
You will cast out all our sins into the depths of the sea pictures complete, irreversible forgiveness; the verb for vanquish or subdue our iniquities carries the sense of treading them underfoot.
